items.content: The fields unspooled past the window like something being slowly remembered, green giving way to amber, then to the dark geometry of plowed earth. She pressed her forehead against the glass and felt the cold vibration of the train moving through her skull. Every small town that flickered by — a grain elevator, a tilted water tower, a row of houses with their backs turned to the tracks — seemed to exist in a time she had no right to witness.

items.content: The streets had narrowed somehow, or perhaps she had simply grown larger in the years between. She walked past the bakery, the pharmacy, the rusted bench where adolescence had unraveled itself in long, restless afternoons, and felt the strange doubling of being both stranger and native at once. Everything was achingly familiar yet faintly wrong, like a song played in the right key but at the wrong tempo — close enough to break your heart, but not quite close enough to mend it.

items.content: Once upon a time and a very good time it was there was a moocow coming down along the road and this moocow that was coming down along the road met a nicens little boy named baby tuckoo.

items.content: The train announced itself long before it arrived, a low trembling that seemed to rise from the earth itself rather than from any mechanical thing. Lying still in the darkness, she listened as the sound swelled and then receded, pulling something unnamed behind it like a tide. There was always that particular loneliness in it — the knowledge that somewhere, in the small hours, other lives were in motion, crossing the night toward destinations she would never see.
